articleTitle: BICC's experience of multimedia communications: issues in CSCW
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia and Professional Applications
abstract: Since 1987, a small team from BICC has been looking into CSCW and, more particularly, multimedia communications. BICC was involved in the RACE I project DIMUN. The focus of the DIMUN project was to discover how to use multimedia communications to allow a group of people who are geographically separated to work together as effectively as a group working together in a single room. As a result of the success of DIMUN, BICC joined a RACE application pilot called BRICC (Broadband Integrated Communications in Construction). This has two aims; to reproduce the DIMUN results using ISDN, and to address the requirements of Balfour Beatty, the construction arm of the BICC Group: As a result of these projects, BICC has become aware of some of the critical issues in the application of CSCW. In this paper the author looks at these. The issues are broken down into a number of areas-need, quality, usability, control and security.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia and Professional Applications
abstract: Electron microscopy has been traditionally associated with complex instruments, to be operated by highly trained specialists only. By borrowing techniques from the multimedia world and by paying much attention to the user interface, an electron microscope can be made simple to use by professionals with limited time. Scanning electron microscopy is, strictly speaking, not multimedia in the traditional sense of the word. Applying multimedia techniques has pushed microscopy from the specialist's domain to well within the scientist's reach.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia and Professional Applications
abstract: Multimedia technologies will revolutionise the way in which information processing is done. In order to develop multimedia applications, powerful processors and high-speed communication networks will have to be installed. In order to develop and maintain multimedia systems, new software and information engineering methods and tools must be developed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The CAR system: multimedia in support of collaborative design
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia and Professional Applications
abstract: With the advent of ISDN, practical wide area multimedia conferencing has become possible at reasonable costs. One such prototype system is the CAR multimedia conferencing system. (CAR stands for 'CAD/CAM for the Automotive industry under the RACE programme'). This system is aimed at assisting distributed collaborative design in the automotive industry. It runs over basic rate ISDN lines or Internet protocol packet networks, with video and audio either provided by integrated video switching and ISDN video codecs, or at lower quality, by software running on the workstation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Opportunities for the application of multimedia technology in medical imaging
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia and Professional Applications
abstract: Various types of equipment and associated software for medical imaging offer integrated functionality for the acquisition, processing, storage and retrieval, presentation, analysis, and hard-copy of images which have been recorded from the inside of the human body. Such images may be used, for example, to diagnose illnesses, to provide guidance during interventions, to plan and execute surgery, and to plan and execute radiation treatment. The all-encompassing goal of the application of these systems is the improvement of the quality and efficiency of health care. Several ideas are presented for multimedia-like functionality which is regarded as useful to the medical imaging environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia and Professional Applications
abstract: This paper is about the impact of multimedia on the professional communicator. A major development in the way multimedia will change over the next few years is the high-definition TV race to produce a new standard that will bring our computer displays and our domestic televisions into complete harmony for the first time. When this happens you can expect computer displays with what will look like cinema resolution in full colour, which are also complete televisions in their own right. Gone will be the problems of flicker and PAL colour shimmer; faster processors will produce real-time antialiasing to guarantee best quality images; and the film industry will find itself under severe pressure to change to the new technology because of the lower cost of video-based rather than film-based productions. This will bring associated benefits for what are presently difficult tasks-dedicated processors for complete computer-recorded video and audio.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multimedia and Professional Applications
abstract: Although technology itself cannot be defined as multimedia, it does form a very important part in the development of multimedia systems. In order to understand how multimedia may be used for information management it is useful to first look at the various components of a typical system. Generally speaking, a multimedia system may be broken down into information sources; hardware and software platform; different media; the application; tools for creating the application; and user interface considerations. If multimedia may be defined at all, it must be in relation to the effective communication and access of information. In short, multimedia could be defined as a tool for information management.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
